steps.text: Colours have names. Look at each one and say its name out loud together:
REDYELLOWBLUE
The first one is RED — like a strawberry 🍓. Say it: “red!”

questions.text: Your turn! Tap the RED one.

options.hint: That's YELLOW — like the sun ☀️. Look for the one that looks like a strawberry 🍓.

options.praise: ⭐ YES! That's RED — like a strawberry! Colour name learned!

options.hint: That's BLUE — like the sky. Look for the strawberry colour 🍓.

rounds.q: Your turn! Tap the YELLOW one — the sun colour.
rounds.praise: ⭐ YES! YELLOW — like the sun! Next colour…

hints.1: That's RED — the strawberry colour. Find YELLOW, like the sun!
hints.2: That's BLUE — the sky colour. Find YELLOW, like the sun!

rounds.q: Now tap the BLUE one — the sky colour.
rounds.praise: ⭐ YES! BLUE — like the sky! One more…

hints.0: That's YELLOW — the sun colour. Find BLUE, like the sky!
hints.1: That's RED — the strawberry colour. Find BLUE, like the sky!

steps.text: Shapes have names too. A circle is round like a ball. A square has 4 straight sides. A triangle has 3 pointy corners — count them: 1, 2, 3!
Circle Square Triangle

questions.text: Your turn! Tap the TRIANGLE — the one with 3 pointy corners.

options.hint: That's the CIRCLE — it's round like a ball, no corners. A triangle has 3 pointy corners!

options.praise: ⭐ YES! TRIANGLE — 1, 2, 3 pointy corners! Shape name learned!

options.hint: That's the SQUARE — it has 4 sides. The triangle has 3 pointy corners!

rounds.q: Your turn! Tap the CIRCLE — round like a ball, no corners.
rounds.praise: ⭐ YES! CIRCLE — round like a ball! Now let's find another shape…

hints.1: That's the TRIANGLE — it has 3 pointy corners. The circle is round like a ball, no corners!
hints.2: That's the SQUARE — 4 straight sides. The circle is round like a ball!

rounds.q: Now tap the SQUARE — 4 straight sides.
rounds.praise: ⭐ YES! SQUARE — 1, 2, 3, 4 straight sides! One more shape…

hints.0: That's the CIRCLE — it's round, no sides. The square has 4 straight sides!
hints.1: That's the TRIANGLE — only 3 sides. The square has 4!

steps.text: Counting means touching each thing one time and saying its number. Tap every apple and count out loud with Hoot:
One tap, one number — that's counting!

questions.text: Your turn! ⭐⭐⭐ — how many stars are there?

options.hint: Count them one at a time, touching each star: 1… 2… one more!

options.praise: ⭐ YES! 1, 2, 3 stars! You counted them!

options.hint: Too many! Touch each star as you count: 1, 2… and one more makes…?

steps.text: Letters make sounds. Say each sound out loud together:
A 🍎A says “ah” — Apple B 🎈B says “buh” — Balloon C 🐱C says “kuh” — Cat

questions.text: Your turn! Which letter says “buh”?

options.hint: A says “ah” — like Apple 🍎. Which letter is for Balloon 🎈?

options.praise: ⭐ YES! B says “buh” — Balloon! First letter sound learned!

options.hint: C says “kuh” — like Cat 🐱. “Buh” is the Balloon letter!

hints.0: That's A — A says “ah”. Listen: which one says “kuh”?
hints.1: That's B — B says “buh”. Listen: which one says “kuh”?
That's B — B says “buh”. Which one says “ah”?
hints.2: That's C — C says “kuh”. Which one says “ah”?

steps.text: Some things are BIG and some are small. Look — say it out loud together:
🐘BIG elephant 🐭small mouse
The elephant takes up lots of room. The mouse takes up just a tiny bit!

questions.text: Your turn! Tap the BIG one.

options.hint: That's the mouse — it's SMALL and tiny. Look for the one that takes up lots of room!

options.praise: ⭐ YES! The ELEPHANT is BIG — it takes up lots of room! Big and small learned!

options.hint: That's an ant — the smallest one of all! The BIG one is much, much larger.

rounds.q: Your turn! Which one is the SMALLEST — the tiniest of all?
rounds.praise: ⭐ YES! The ANT is the smallest! Now find the BIG one…

hints.0: The mouse is small — but look for something even tinier!
hints.1: The elephant is BIG! Find the tiniest one.

steps.text: Counting can go backwards too — like a rocket getting ready to launch! Say it out loud together, slower and quieter… then BLAST OFF:
Each number is one LESS than the one before it.

questions.text: 5…❓Your turn! Counting back: 5… what comes next?

options.hint: 6 is one MORE than 5 — that's counting forwards! Counting back means one LESS.

options.praise: ⭐ YES! 5… 4! One less! You're ready for blast off!

options.hint: 3 comes later — you skipped one! After 5 comes the number just one less: 5, then…?

steps.text: Three more letters, three more sounds. Say them out loud together:
D 🐶D says “duh” — Dog F 🐸F says “fff” — Frog G 🍇G says “guh” — Grapes

questions.text: Your turn! Which letter says “duh”?

options.hint: F says “fff” — like Frog 🐸. “Duh” is the Dog letter!

options.praise: ⭐ YES! D says “duh” — Dog! Another letter sound learned!

options.hint: G says “guh” — like Grapes 🍇. Which letter starts Dog?

hints.1: That's D — D says “duh”. Which one says “fff”?
hints.2: That's G — G says “guh”. Which one says “fff”?

hints.0: That's F — F says “fff”. Which one says “guh”?
hints.1: That's D — D says “duh”. Which one says “guh”?

steps.text: Sorting means putting things that are the same together. Look: all the RED things go in one pile, all the BLUE things in another:
🔴 Red pile🍎 🚗 🎈 🔵 Blue pile🧢 🐳 🫐
Everything in a pile matches that pile's colour!

questions.text: Your turn! Here comes a RED strawberry 🍓. Which pile does it go in?

options.hint: The strawberry is RED — the blue pile is only for blue things. Match the colour!

options.praise: ⭐ YES! Red goes with red — you sorted it! Sorting star earned!

options.hint: Nothing goes on the floor — everything has a pile where it matches. The strawberry is red, so…?

steps.text: After 5, the numbers keep going: 6, 7, 8, 9, 10! Tap every star and count all the way up with Hoot:
One tap, one number — all the way to 10!

questions.text: Your turn! 🐥🐥🐥🐥🐥🐥🐥🐥 — how many ducklings are there?

options.hint: Count them one at a time, touching each duckling: 1… 2… keep going past 5!

options.praise: ⭐ YES! 8 ducklings — you counted past 5! Counting to 10 learned!

options.hint: Too many! Touch each duckling as you count and stop at the last one: …6, 7, and one more!

steps.text: Three more colours to name. Say each one out loud together:
GREENORANGEPURPLE
GREEN is grass 🌱, ORANGE is an orange 🍊, and PURPLE is grapes 🍇!

questions.text: Your turn! Tap the GREEN one — the grass colour.

options.hint: That's PURPLE — like grapes 🍇. Green is the colour of grass 🌱.
That's ORANGE — like an orange 🍊. Look for the grass colour 🌱.

options.praise: ⭐ YES! That's GREEN — like grass! Three new colours learned!

rounds.q: Your turn! Tap the ORANGE one — like an orange!
rounds.praise: ⭐ YES! ORANGE — like an orange! Next colour…

hints.0: That's PURPLE — like grapes. Find ORANGE!
hints.2: That's GREEN — the grass colour. Find ORANGE!

rounds.q: Now tap the PURPLE one — like grapes.
rounds.praise: ⭐ YES! PURPLE — like grapes! One more…

hints.1: That's ORANGE. Find PURPLE, like grapes!
hints.2: That's GREEN — the grass colour. Find PURPLE, like grapes!

steps.text: Every animal has its own sound. Make them together — as loud as you like!
🐮Cow says “moo!” 🦆Duck says “quack!” 🐶Dog says “woof!”

questions.text: Your turn! Who says “moo”?

options.hint: The duck says “quack!” 🦆. “Moo” is a big farm animal with horns.

options.praise: ⭐ YES! The COW says “moo!” Animal sounds learned!

options.hint: The dog says “woof!” 🐶. Who says “moo” on the farm?

rounds.praise: ⭐ YES! The DUCK says quack! Next one…

hints.1: The COW says moo. Who says quack?
hints.2: The DOG says woof. Who says quack?

rounds.praise: ⭐ YES! The DOG says woof! One more…

hints.0: The DUCK says quack. Who says woof?
hints.1: The COW says moo. Who says woof?

steps.text: Faces show feelings. Look at each face and make it on your own face too!
😀HAPPY — big smile 😢Sad — wobbly mouth 😴Sleepy — closing eyes
Feelings are okay to have — and okay to say out loud: “I feel happy!”

questions.text: Your turn! Tap the HAPPY face — the one with the big smile.

options.hint: That face is SAD 😢. Happy has a big smile — find the smiliest one!
That face is SLEEPY 😴 — its eyes are closing. Happy is wide awake and smiling!

options.praise: ⭐ YES! That's the HAPPY face — big smile! Feelings learned!

rounds.q: Your turn! Tap the SAD face — the wobbly mouth.
rounds.praise: ⭐ YES! That face is SAD. It's OK to feel sad — a hug helps. One more…

hints.1: That face is SLEEPY — eyes closed. Find the SAD one, with the wobbly mouth.
hints.2: That face is HAPPY — big smile. Find the SAD one, with the wobbly mouth.

steps.text: Some things are UP high, and some are DOWN low. Point up, then point down as you say them:
⬆️ 🐦UP — bird in the sky ⬇️ 🐜DOWN — ant on the ground

questions.text: Your turn! Tap the one that is UP.

options.praise: ⭐ YES! The BIRD is UP in the sky! Up and down learned!

options.hint: The ant is DOWN low on the ground 🐜. UP is high, high above your head!
The worm is DOWN under the ground 🪱. Look for the one flying high in the sky!

rounds.q: Your turn! Which one is UNDER the ground?
rounds.praise: ⭐ YES! The WORM lives under the ground! Now find one that is UP…

hints.0: The bird is UP in the sky. Who is under the ground?
hints.1: The ant walks ON the ground. Who is UNDER it?

steps.text: A pattern repeats the same thing, over and over. Look and say it out loud:
Red, blue, red, blue… after blue always comes red again! The pattern tells you what is next.

questions.text: Your turn! 🍎 🍌 🍎 🍌 🍎 … what comes next?

options.hint: Grapes aren't in this pattern at all! The pattern only uses apple, banana, apple, banana…
The apple just came! The pattern takes turns: apple, banana, apple, banana — so after apple comes…?

options.praise: ⭐ YES! Apple, banana, apple, banana — BANANA comes next! Patterns learned!

steps.text: Your body parts each have a job. Touch each one as Hoot names it:
👀EYES are for seeing 👂EARS are for hearing 👃NOSE is for smelling

questions.text: Your turn! Hoot is playing a song 🎵. What do you hear it with?

options.hint: Eyes are for SEEING 👀. A song is a sound — which body part catches sounds?

options.praise: ⭐ YES! Your EARS hear the song! Body parts learned!

options.hint: Your nose is for SMELLING 👃 — flowers and cookies! Music goes in a different part.

rounds.q: Your turn! What do you SEE a picture with?
rounds.praise: ⭐ YES! We SEE with our EYES! Next one…

hints.1: EARS are for hearing. What do you SEE with?
hints.2: Your NOSE is for smelling. What do you SEE with?

rounds.q: What do you SMELL a flower with?
rounds.praise: ⭐ YES! We SMELL with our NOSE! One more…

hints.0: EYES are for seeing. What do you SMELL with?
hints.1: EARS are for hearing. What do you SMELL with?

steps.text: Two more shapes to know! A star has 5 pointy points — count them: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5! A heart is round on top and pointy at the bottom.
Star Heart

questions.text: Your turn! Tap the STAR — the one with 5 pointy points.

options.hint: That's the HEART — round on top, one point at the bottom. The star has FIVE points!
That's the CIRCLE — round all the way, no points at all. Count the star's points: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5!

options.praise: ⭐ YES! STAR — 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 pointy points! You finished all 16 Little Explorers lessons — superstar!

rounds.q: Your turn! Tap the HEART — the love shape.
rounds.praise: ⭐ YES! HEART — the love shape! Next shape…

hints.1: That's a CIRCLE — round, no points. Find the HEART!
hints.2: That's the STAR — 5 points. Find the HEART!

rounds.q: Now tap the CIRCLE — round like a ball.
rounds.praise: ⭐ YES! CIRCLE — round like a ball! One more…

hints.0: That's the HEART. Find the round CIRCLE!
hints.2: That's the STAR — pointy. Find the round CIRCLE!

steps.text: Every letter makes its own sound. Say them out loud:
S 🐍“sss” — like a snake M 🐮“mmm” — like yummy food T 🐢“tuh” — a tiny tap sound
Reading starts here: know the sound, and you can start sounding out whole words.

questions.text: Your turn! Which letter makes the “sss” snake sound?

options.hint: M says “mmm”. The snake sound “sss” belongs to another letter — which one hisses?

options.praise: ⭐ YES! S says “sss” — like a snake! Letter sound learned!

options.hint: T says “tuh”. Listen for the hiss: “sss…” — which letter is the snake's?

options.t: Every letter makes its own sound — S says “sss” like a snake.
All letters make the same sound.
options.fix: Not quite! If all letters sounded the same, we couldn't read words. Remember the chips: S hisses “sss”, M hums “mmm”, T taps “tuh” — every letter has its OWN sound. Pick the sentence that says that!

options.t: Letters are just pictures to look at.
options.fix: Not quite — letters aren't just pictures! Each letter stands for a sound you say out loud: S says “sss”. Pick the sentence that tells Hoot that!

steps.text: Blending means pushing letter sounds together until they become one word. Watch:
c … a … t → caaat → CAT 🐱
Say the sounds slowly, then faster and faster — the word pops out! This is how ALL reading works.

questions.text: Your turn! Push these together: m … a … p. What word do you get?

options.hint: Say it slowly: mmm…aaa…p. What do you use to find treasure?

options.praise: ⭐ YES! m-a-p blends into MAP! You just read a word!

options.hint: That word ends in “n”. Our sounds end in “p”: m…a…p…

options.t: Push the sounds together — slow, then faster — and they pop into a word: m…a…p makes MAP!
Say each sound on its own and stop — the word stays in pieces.
options.fix: Not quite — stopping between sounds keeps the word in pieces! Blending means NO gaps: say m…a…p faster and faster until MAP pops out. Pick the sentence that says that!

options.t: Blending means mixing the letters up in any order.
options.fix: Not quite — the sounds stay in order! m first, a next, p last: m…a…p. Push them together in that order and you get MAP.

steps.text: Adding trick: don't start from 1 — start from the big number and count on. Watch 3 + 2:
Hold “3” in your head… then count on for the red dots: 4, 5! So 3 + 2 = 5.

questions.text: Your turn! 4 + 2 = ? Hold 4 in your head, then count on two more.

options.hint: Start at 4 and count on: the next number is 5… and one more after that?

options.praise: ⭐ YES! 4… 5, 6! 4 + 2 = 6. Counting on works!

options.hint: You counted on three. We only add 2: 4… 5, and one more.

options.t: Start at the big number and count on — don't go back to 1.
Always start counting from 1, every time.
options.fix: Not quite — starting back at 1 is the slow way! Hold the big number in your head: for 4 + 2, start at 4 and count on — 5, 6! Pick the sentence that says that!

options.t: Counting on means counting the big number again and again.
options.fix: Not quite — the big number is already counted inside your head. You only count the NEW ones on: 4 in your head, then 5, 6.

lessons.title: Read a line — and understand it

steps.text: Reading isn't just saying words — it's picturing what they mean. Read this line out loud, word by word:
The cat sat on the mat.
Now picture it: a cat, sitting, on a mat. If you can see the picture in your head, you truly read it!

questions.text: Your turn! In that line, WHO sat on the mat?

options.praise: ⭐ YES! The CAT sat on the mat — you read it AND understood it!

options.hint: There's no dog in the line. Read it again slowly: “The … sat on the mat.”
The mat is what got sat ON. Who did the sitting? Read the first words again.

options.t: Reading means picturing it in your head — who is there, and what is happening.
Reading is only saying the words out loud.
options.fix: Not quite — just saying the words isn't really reading yet! You truly read it when you can PICTURE it: the cat, sitting, on the mat.

options.t: The mat did the sitting in the line.
options.fix: Not quite — the mat got sat ON! The CAT did the sitting. Good readers picture who does what — pick the sentence that says that!

steps.text: Words rhyme when they end with the same sound. Listen: cat and hat both end in “at” — they rhyme! So do sun and run, with their “un” ending. Rhyming words are word cousins — and hearing rhymes makes reading easier.

questions.text: Your turn! Which word rhymes with DOG?

options.hint: CAT ends in “at” — that's the cat/hat rhyme family. DOG ends in “og”… which word ends the same way?

options.praise: ⭐ YES! DOG and LOG both end in “og” — they rhyme!

options.hint: SUN ends in “un” — it rhymes with RUN. DOG's rhyme has to end in “og”.

options.t: Rhyming words end with the same sound — DOG and LOG both end in “og”.
Rhyming words start with the same sound.
options.fix: Not quite — rhymes match at the END, not the start! Listen to the tails: d-OG and l-OG end the same way. Pick the sentence that says that!

options.t: Words rhyme when they look the same on the page.
options.fix: Not quite — trust your ears, not your eyes! Rhyming is about the SOUND at the end: DOG and LOG sound the same at the end, so they rhyme.

steps.text: Adding puts more in. Taking away leaves less. Start with 5 apples and take 2 away to eat:
Count what's left: 1, 2, 3. So 5 − 2 = 3. The faded apples are the ones that got eaten!

questions.text: Your turn! 6 − 2 = ? Start at 6, take 2 away, count what's left.

options.hint: That's how many you took away. The question asks how many are LEFT: 6… take away 1 (that's 5), take away 1 more (that's…?).

options.praise: ⭐ YES! 6 take away 2 leaves 4! Taking away works!

options.hint: That's taking away only 1. We take away TWO: 6, then 5, then one more…

options.t: Taking away means some leave — then you count what is LEFT.
Taking away means counting the ones that left.
options.fix: Not quite — the ones that left are gone! The answer is what's still there: 6 take away 2 leaves 4. Count the ones LEFT — pick the sentence that says that!

options.t: After taking away, there is more than you started with.
options.fix: Not quite — taking away makes LESS, never more! Start with everything, take the leaving ones away, and count what's left.

steps.text: Big numbers are built from tens and ones. Look at 14: it is ONE bundle of ten, plus 4 loose ones:
🧺 101 ten+🍎🍎🍎🍎4 ones
The first digit tells the tens, the last digit tells the ones. That's the secret code inside every number!

questions.text: Your turn! In the number 23, how many TENS are there?

options.hint: 3 is the last digit — those are the ONES. The FIRST digit tells the tens.

options.praise: ⭐ YES! 23 = 2 tens and 3 ones. You cracked the number code!

options.hint: 23 is the whole number, not the tens. Split it up: how many bundles of ten fit inside 23?

options.t: The first digit tells the tens and the last digit tells the ones — 23 is 2 tens and 3 ones.
The last digit tells the tens.
options.fix: Not quite — it's the other way round! The FIRST digit counts the bundles of ten, and the LAST digit counts the loose ones: 23 = 2 tens and 3 ones.

options.t: 23 is just 23 ones, with no tens inside.
options.fix: Not quite — bundles of ten hide inside big numbers! 23 holds 2 whole tens (that's 20) plus 3 loose ones. Pick the sentence that says that!

steps.text: Good readers can answer questions about what they read — the answers hide INSIDE the words. Read this line out loud:
The frog jumped into the pond.
Picture it: a frog, a big jump, a splash! Now hunt for the answer in the line.

questions.text: Your turn! WHERE did the frog jump?

options.hint: There's no log in the line. Read it again and look for the place words: “into the …”

options.praise: ⭐ YES! “Into the pond” — the answer was hiding right there in the line!

options.hint: The frog in this line jumps into water, not up a tree. Read the last words again: “into the …”

options.t: The answers hide inside the line — a WHERE question wants a place, like “into the pond”.
You guess the answer without looking at the line.
options.fix: Not quite — good readers don't guess! The answer is hiding IN the words: “into the pond” was right there in the line. Pick the sentence that says that!

options.t: A WHERE question wants a person.
options.fix: Not quite — WHERE asks for a PLACE! WHO wants a person or an animal. Listen to the question word, then hunt for that kind of word in the line.

steps.text: 3 × 4 means 3 groups of 4. Look at the dots — 3 rows of 4:
Count them in 4s: 4, 8, 12. So 3 × 4 = 12. Any times table is just groups you can count — you never have to guess.

questions.text: Your challenge! 5 × 3 = ? (5 groups of 3 — count in 3s: 3, 6, 9…)

options.hint: That's 5 + 3. Multiplying means GROUPS: count five 3s — 3, 6, 9, 12… one more!

options.praise: ⭐ YES! 3, 6, 9, 12, 15 — 5 × 3 = 15! Groups mastered!

options.hint: You counted four 3s. 5 × 3 needs FIVE groups of 3: 3, 6, 9, 12, …

options.t: A times table is just equal groups you can count — 3 × 4 is 3 groups of 4: count in 4s — 4, 8, 12.
Multiplying is adding the two numbers together.
options.fix: Not quite — 3 × 4 is not 3 + 4! Multiplying builds GROUPS: 3 groups of 4. Count the groups in 4s — 4, 8, 12 — and you never have to guess. Pick the sentence that says that!

options.t: Times tables can only be memorised — there is no way to work them out.
options.fix: Not quite — there IS a way to work every one out! Each table is groups you can count: 5 × 3 is five 3s — 3, 6, 9, 12, 15. Pick the sentence that says that!

steps.text: A fraction is a whole cut into equal parts. This pizza is cut in half — each piece is 1/2. Cut it into 4 and each piece is 1/4:
1/2 — one of 2 parts 1/4 — one of 4 parts
The trick everyone trips on: more parts means each part is SMALLER. So 1/2 is bigger than 1/4 — even though 4 is bigger than 2!

questions.text: Your challenge! Which is the bigger slice?

options.praise: ⭐ YES! 1/2 wins — fewer parts, bigger slices! Fractions understood!

options.hint: Careful — that's the trap! Cut into 4, every slice gets SMALLER. Which cut makes the biggest pieces?
They're not equal — look at the pizzas above. The half slice is much bigger than a quarter slice.

options.t: A fraction is a whole cut into EQUAL parts — and the more parts you cut, the smaller each part is, so 1/2 is bigger than 1/4.
1/4 is bigger than 1/2, because 4 is bigger than 2.
options.fix: That's the trap this lesson warned about! The bottom number counts the parts — MORE parts means each part is SMALLER. Cut into 2 and the slices are big; cut into 4 and they shrink. Pick the sentence that says that!

options.t: The parts of a fraction don't have to be equal, as long as they make the whole.
options.fix: Not quite — EQUAL parts are the whole point of a fraction! If the pieces aren't equal, you can't call each one a quarter. Pick the sentence that says the parts are equal!

steps.text: Strong readers ask: what is this whole text about? That's the main idea. Read this:
“Deep under a volcano, rock melts into magma. Pressure builds and builds — until the magma bursts out as lava, ash and gas. That explosion is an eruption.”
“Lava is hot” is true, but it's just one detail. The whole text explains one thing: how a volcano erupts.

questions.text: Your challenge! What is the main idea of that text?

options.hint: True — but that's one small detail. The main idea covers the WHOLE text, beginning to end.

options.praise: ⭐ YES! Magma, pressure, eruption — the whole text is about how volcanoes erupt!

options.hint: The text never talks about old rocks. Ask: what does EVERY sentence help explain?

options.t: The main idea is what the WHOLE text is about — every sentence works together to explain that one thing.
The main idea is the most interesting detail in the text.
options.fix: Not quite — “Lava is very hot” is a real detail, but it's only ONE piece. The main idea covers the WHOLE text, beginning to end: how a volcano erupts. Pick the sentence that says that!

options.t: The main idea is always stated in the first sentence.
options.fix: Not quite — the first sentence can open the topic without stating the point. Ask what EVERY sentence helps explain — magma, pressure, bursting out — and that's the main idea.

steps.text: Code is a list of instructions a computer follows exactly, in order. This code — ➡ ➡ ⬆ — moves Hoot right, right, up. Swap the order and Hoot ends up somewhere completely different. Programmers plan the whole path before pressing run.

questions.text: Your challenge! Hoot needs to go UP first, then RIGHT. Which code does that?

options.hint: That code goes RIGHT first. Hoot needs to go UP before he goes right.

options.praise: ⭐ YES! ⬆ then ➡ — up first, then right. You think like a coder!

options.hint: That starts by going DOWN — the wrong way entirely! Hoot's first step is UP.

options.t: Code is a list of instructions a computer follows exactly, in order — swap the order and you end up somewhere completely different.
A computer figures out what you meant, even if the steps are in the wrong order.
options.fix: Not quite — computers don't guess what you mean! They follow the list exactly as written, step by step — so ⬆ then ➡ lands somewhere different from ➡ then ⬆. Pick the sentence that says that!

options.t: The order of the steps only matters at the start of a program.
options.fix: Not quite — order matters for EVERY step, because each step starts from where the last one ended. Change any step's place and the whole path changes.

steps.text: Dividing is sharing equally — the opposite of multiplying. Share 12 cookies fairly between 3 friends: deal them out one at a time — round 1, round 2, round 3, round 4 — and each friend ends with 4. So 12 ÷ 3 = 4. Check it with your times tables: 3 × 4 = 12 ✓. Division and multiplication are a team.

questions.text: Your challenge! 20 stickers shared equally among 4 friends. How many does each friend get?

options.hint: Check with multiplication: 4 × 4 = 16, not 20. Each friend needs one more round of dealing.

options.praise: ⭐ YES! 4 × 5 = 20, so 20 ÷ 4 = 5 stickers each. Fair shares!

options.hint: Too many — 4 × 6 = 24, more stickers than we have. Deal out 20 between 4 friends and count the rounds.

options.t: Dividing means sharing equally — and you can check it with multiplication: 20 ÷ 4 = 5 because 4 × 5 = 20.
Dividing means taking things away until nothing is left.
options.fix: Not quite — division isn't about what's taken away, it's about FAIR SHARES. Deal 20 stickers to 4 friends one at a time and each friend ends with 5. Pick the sentence that says that!

options.t: Division and multiplication are separate tricks that have nothing to do with each other.
options.fix: Not quite — they're a team! Multiplication builds the groups and division shares them back out, so one always checks the other: 3 × 4 = 12 means 12 ÷ 3 = 4.

steps.text: Plants are food factories that run on sunshine. It's called photosynthesis: the roots drink water, the leaves catch sunlight and breathe in air — and the plant turns them into its own food, releasing the oxygen we breathe out the other side. Nearly every meal you have ever eaten started inside a leaf!

questions.text: Your challenge! What do leaves mainly catch, to make the plant's food?

options.praise: ⭐ YES! Sunlight powers the whole factory — photosynthesis understood!

options.hint: Water matters, but the ROOTS drink it — leaves don't catch it to make food. What shines down on leaves all day?
Leaves aren't bug traps (one rare plant aside!). Think about what every leaf is facing, all day long.

options.t: In photosynthesis, a plant turns sunlight, water and air into its own food — and releases oxygen while it does it.
Plants take their food ready-made from the soil, the way animals eat a meal.
options.fix: Not quite — plants MAKE their food; they don't eat it! The roots only drink water. The leaves catch sunlight and turn water and air into food — that's photosynthesis.

options.t: Photosynthesis is how plants breathe while they sleep.
options.fix: Not quite — photosynthesis is food-making, and it runs on SUNLIGHT, so it happens in the light: leaves catch the light and turn it into food, letting oxygen out.

steps.text: A paragraph has ONE main idea, and its first sentence — the topic sentence — announces it. Read: “Bees are tiny flying farmers. One bee visits about 50 flowers on a single trip, carrying pollen from flower to flower as it goes…” Everything after the first sentence works to prove it. A weak opener like “Bees are insects” announces nothing worth proving.

questions.text: Your challenge! Which is the strongest topic sentence for a paragraph about how dogs help people?

options.text: Dogs are animals with four legs.
options.hint: True, but it announces nothing to prove — any paragraph at all could follow it. A topic sentence makes a claim the paragraph then backs up.

options.text: Dogs help people as guides, guards and rescue partners.
options.praise: ⭐ YES! A real claim — now the whole paragraph can prove it with examples. Topic sentence mastered!

options.text: My dog is the best dog ever.
options.hint: That's a feeling about one dog, not an idea a paragraph can explore and prove. Look for the sentence with a job to do.

options.t: A topic sentence opens a paragraph by announcing its one main idea as a claim — and every sentence after it works to prove that claim.
A topic sentence is any true fact about the topic.
options.fix: Not quite — “Bees are insects” is true, but it announces nothing worth proving. A real topic sentence makes a claim — “Bees are tiny flying farmers” — that the whole paragraph then backs up. Pick the sentence that says that!

options.t: A topic sentence belongs at the end, where it sums the paragraph up.
options.fix: Not quite — a summary can close a paragraph, but the topic sentence OPENS it: it tells the reader the one main idea up front, and everything after it proves that idea.

steps.text: Area measures how much flat space something covers — counted in squares. This rug is 4 squares long and 3 squares wide:
Count them: 12 squares. The fast way is length × width: 4 × 3 = 12. Rows times columns, every time.

questions.text: Your challenge! A garden is 5 squares long and 2 squares wide. What is its area?

options.hint: 7 is 5 + 2 — that's adding the sides. Area MULTIPLIES length × width: picture two rows of 5 squares.

options.praise: ⭐ YES! 5 × 2 = 10 squares of garden. Area mastered!

options.hint: That's the rug from the lesson (4 × 3). This garden is 5 × 2 — count two rows of five.

options.t: Area measures the flat space a shape covers, counted in squares — and you find it with length × width: 4 × 3 = 12 squares.
You find area by adding the length and the width together.
options.fix: Not quite — adding walks along two sides: 5 + 2 = 7. Area counts the SQUARES covering the surface: two rows of 5 squares is 5 × 2 = 10. Pick the sentence that says that!

options.t: Area measures the distance around the edge of a shape.
options.fix: Not quite — the distance around the edge is the perimeter. Area is the space INSIDE the shape, counted in squares — rows times columns, length × width.

steps.text: Your lemonade recipe is a ratio: 2 cups lemon : 3 cups water. Making a double batch? Double both sides — 4 : 6 — and it tastes identical. Scale only one side and the ratio breaks. Every recipe, map, model and mix in your projects works this way.

questions.text: Your call! You're scaling up to 12 cups of water. How much lemon keeps the taste the same?

options.hint: That's doubling the lemon, but the water went ×4 (3 → 12), not ×2. Both sides must scale by the SAME number.

options.praise: ⭐ YES! Water ×4 means lemon ×4: 2 × 4 = 8. Ratio held!

options.hint: That's adding the same amount to both sides — ratios don't work by adding. They scale by MULTIPLYING both sides equally.

options.t: A ratio stays the same only when BOTH sides are multiplied by the same number — 2 : 3 scaled by 4 becomes 8 : 12.
A ratio stays the same if you add the same amount to both sides.
options.fix: Not quite — adding changes the relationship: 2 : 3 with 9 added to both sides is 11 : 12, a completely different mix. Ratios scale by multiplying both sides by the same number.

options.t: To make a bigger batch, scale up the side you need more of.
options.fix: Not quite — scaling one side alone breaks the ratio and changes the taste. Whatever multiplier the water gets, the lemon gets too: 3 → 12 is ×4, so 2 cups of lemon becomes 8.

steps.text: Before any fact goes into your project, run the 3 checks: 1) Who wrote it — an expert or organisation you can name? 2) Can another source confirm it? 3) Is it informing you — or selling to you? A source that passes all three earns its place; one that fails gets dropped, however cool it sounds.

questions.text: Your call! Which source is strongest for the Volcano Lab?

options.text: A comment under a volcano video
options.hint: Run the checks: who wrote it? Nobody you can name — and nothing confirms it. Comments are opinions, not sources.

options.text: A geologist's page on a university website
options.praise: ⭐ YES! Named experts, checkable, informing not selling — all 3 checks passed!

options.text: An advert for a volcano toy kit
options.hint: Check 3 fails: it's SELLING volcano toys. Ads can spark ideas, but they're not evidence.

options.t: A source earns trust by passing three checks: a named, credible author; confirmation from another source; and a purpose of informing, not selling.
A source is trustworthy if it sounds confident and detailed.
options.fix: Not quite — confidence is not one of the checks. Run the three: WHO wrote it — can you name them? Can another source CONFIRM it? Is it informing you, or SELLING to you? A polished advert fails them.

options.t: The newest source is automatically the most trustworthy.
options.fix: Not quite — newness is not one of the checks either. A university page by a named geologist passes all three; a brand-new anonymous comment passes none.

steps.text: The maker's rule when something breaks: change ONE thing, retest, write down what happened. Change three things at once and the build might work — but you'll never know which change fixed it, so you'll be stuck again next time.

questions.text: Your call! In your game, the jump is broken AND the sprite is the wrong colour. What's the first move?

options.text: Fix the jump only, retest, then the colour
options.praise: ⭐ YES! One fix, one retest — you'll know exactly what worked. That's debugging!

options.text: Change both at the same time
options.hint: Tempting — but if the game then works, which change fixed it? You'd never know. One thing at a time.

options.text: Delete it and start the game over
options.hint: Starting over throws away everything that already works. Makers isolate the fault first: one change, one retest.

options.t: When something breaks, change ONE thing, retest, and write down what happened — that is the only way to know which change actually fixed it.
Changing several things at once is just as good, because it is faster.
options.fix: Not quite — it may be faster, but it teaches you nothing: if the build works afterwards, you cannot say which change fixed it, so you will be stuck again next time. One change, one retest.

options.t: If a build breaks, the safest move is to delete it and start over.
options.fix: Not quite — starting over throws away everything that already works. Isolate the fault instead: one small change, one retest, one note about what happened.

steps.text: Every strong presentation has the same skeleton: HOOK — one line that makes people care. BUILD — show the work, including what went wrong and what you changed. LAND — finish with what you'd do next. Beginning, middle, end — on purpose, not by accident.

questions.text: Your call! Which opening is a real HOOK for the Volcano Lab?

options.text: “First, I will read my list of materials.”
options.hint: That's a list, not a hook — nobody leans in for materials. A hook opens with the most exciting TRUE thing about the work.

options.text: “Um, so… this is my project, I guess.”
options.hint: Honest, but it gives the audience nothing to hold on to. Lead with the result — the moment it all paid off.

options.text: “Our volcano erupted for 40 seconds — here's how we made it do that.”
options.praise: ⭐ YES! A real result, up front — now everyone wants to know HOW. That's a hook!

options.t: A strong presentation runs hook, build, land: open with the result that makes people care, show the work — including what went wrong — and finish with what you would do next.
A strong presentation opens by listing the materials and steps in order.
options.fix: Not quite — a materials list is part of the build, not the opening. The HOOK comes first: the most exciting TRUE result, up front, so the audience leans in to hear how you did it.

options.t: The build should show only what went well, so the work looks polished.
options.fix: Not quite — the build is more convincing WITH the failures: what went wrong and what you changed is the proof the result was earned. Polish belongs to the landing, not to hiding the process.

steps.text: A percent is a slice of 100. The maker's shortcut: find 10% first — just move the decimal one place left — then build up. 10% of 240 playtesters is 24, so 25% is 24 + 24 + 12 = 60. Fundraising goals, discounts, battery bars and test scores all speak percent; now you can speak it back.

questions.text: Your call! 50% of your 80 playtesters finished the demo. How many players is that?

options.hint: That's using 50 as a count of people, not a percent. 50% means exactly HALF — what is half of 80?

options.praise: ⭐ YES! 50% = half: 80 ÷ 2 = 40 players. Percent fluency earned!

options.hint: 30 is less than half of 80. 50% is exactly half — and half of 80 is…?

options.t: A percent is a part of 100 — find 10% first by moving the decimal one place left, then build up to the percent you need.
50% of 80 is 50, because the percent number is the count.
options.fix: Not quite — the percent is a rate out of 100, not a headcount. 50% means exactly half of the whole, whatever the whole is — and half of 80 playtesters is 40.

options.t: To find a percent of a number, multiply the number by the percent and stop there.
options.fix: Not quite — 80 × 50 gives 4,000, more people than exist in the problem. A percent is per hundred: 50 out of every 100 is a half, so find the fraction of the whole — half of 80 is 40.

lessons.title: The design loop: test, fix, retest

steps.text: No first version survives contact with a real user — and that's the plan, not a failure. Professionals work in a loop: sketch it rough → test it on a real person → fix the ONE biggest problem → test again. Polish comes last, never first: a beautiful level nobody can finish is still a broken level.

questions.text: Your call! Your first playtester gets stuck at the level-1 door for two whole minutes. What's the first move?

options.text: Add three more levels so there's more to play
options.hint: More content built behind a door nobody can open just makes a bigger stuck game. Fix the biggest blocker first, then retest the loop.

options.text: Watch where they get stuck, fix just the door, retest
options.praise: ⭐ YES! Watch, fix the door, retest — the design loop in action. That's how real games ship!

options.text: Decide the playtester just isn't good at games
options.hint: The playtester isn't the bug — the door is. When a real user stalls somewhere, the design is telling you something.

options.t: The design loop is: test on a real person, fix the ONE biggest problem you find, then test again — polish comes last, never first.
When a playtester gets stuck, the tester is the problem — find better testers.
options.fix: Not quite — a stuck tester is the design talking to you. The playtester isn't the bug; the door is. Watch where they stall, fix that one thing, and retest the loop.

options.t: Adding more content is the fastest way to improve a design that testers struggle with.
options.fix: Not quite — content built behind a door nobody can open just makes a bigger stuck product. The loop fixes the biggest blocker first, then tests again to prove the fix.

steps.text: Persuasive writing is a claim carrying its proof. Weak: “Our film is the best.” — nothing there can be checked. Strong: “Our film holds attention because every scene ends on an unanswered question — test viewers named the cliffhangers as the reason they kept watching.” Claim, reason, evidence — in one breath.

questions.text: Your call! Which sentence is a claim WITH evidence, for the Backyard Scientist journal?

options.text: “The sunny bed grew 9 cm taller than the shady bed over six weeks, so sunlight drove the growth.”
options.praise: ⭐ YES! Claim, numbers, comparison — evidence doing real work. Argument writing unlocked!

options.hint: An opinion with no measurement behind it — nothing a reader can check. Strong writing attaches numbers or observations to the claim.
That's a diary entry — it records a day but claims nothing. A claim says WHAT something means or WHY, and brings proof.

options.t: A strong claim carries its proof: it states what is true, gives the reason, and attaches evidence a reader can check — numbers, observations, comparisons.
A claim sounds stronger with words like “obviously” doing the persuading.
options.fix: Not quite — “Plants obviously love the sun” gives a reader nothing to check. “The sunny bed grew 9 cm taller than the shady bed” can be verified — evidence, not emphasis, does the persuading.

options.t: A day-by-day diary of what you did counts as evidence for a claim.
options.fix: Not quite — a diary records events but claims nothing. Evidence has to back a CLAIM: the six-week growth comparison is evidence because it supports the statement that sunlight drove the growth.

steps.text: Real projects run on real budgets, and a budget is just careful adding done before you spend. Volcano Lab budget: $60. Already spent: board $25 and paint $20 — that's $45, leaving $15. Every new cost gets checked against what's LEFT, not against the original $60. That one habit is the difference between finished projects and abandoned ones.

questions.text: Your call! The eruption kit costs $12. Can the Volcano Lab afford it?

options.text: No — the kit pushes it over budget
options.hint: Add it up again: 25 + 20 + 12 = 57, and the budget is 60. Recheck before deciding — the numbers say it fits.

options.praise: ⭐ YES! $25 + $20 + $12 = $57 — inside the $60 budget with $3 to spare. Budget kept!

options.text: Yes — and you'll still have $15 left
options.hint: $15 left before the kit is right — but the kit costs $12, which comes OUT of that $15. How much would actually remain?

options.t: Every new cost is checked against what is LEFT of the budget — not against the original total — because money already spent is already gone.
A project is fine as long as each single item costs less than the original budget.
options.fix: Not quite — the $12 kit costs far less than $60, but $45 was already spent. Items are not checked one by one against the original total; they are checked against the $15 that remains.

options.t: What is left of a budget is the original total minus the price of the newest item.
options.fix: Not quite — what is left subtracts EVERYTHING already spent: $60 − $25 − $20 leaves $15. The newest item then comes out of that remainder — $12 out of $15 leaves $3.

steps.text: Every cell runs on ATP — energy currency. The mitochondria mint it: they take glucose from food plus oxygen from breathing and convert them into ATP. Muscles, brain, everything spends it. That's why you breathe faster when you run: your cells are demanding more ATP, so the mitochondria need more oxygen.

questions.text: Check it! Which organelle produces most of a cell's ATP?

options.praise: ⭐ Correct — mitochondria convert glucose + oxygen into ATP. That's how every cell gets its energy.

options.hint: The nucleus stores DNA — it's the instruction library, not the power plant. Which organelle CONVERTS food and oxygen into energy?
Ribosomes build proteins. Energy production happens in a different organelle — the one that uses oxygen.

options.t: The mitochondria produce most of a cell's ATP by converting glucose and oxygen — ATP is the energy currency that every cellular process spends.
The nucleus produces the cell's energy and distributes it to the other organelles.
options.fix: Not quite — the nucleus stores DNA; it is the instruction library, not the power plant. Energy conversion — glucose plus oxygen into ATP — happens in the mitochondria.

options.t: ATP is produced by the lungs during breathing and stored there until cells need it.
options.fix: Not quite — ATP is minted inside the cells themselves, in the mitochondria. Breathing only supplies the oxygen — which is precisely why it speeds up when cellular demand for ATP rises.

steps.text: Solving an equation means getting x alone — and an equation is a balance: whatever you do to one side, you must do to the other. Worked example:
x + 5 = 12 → subtract 5 from BOTH sides → x = 7
Check: 7 + 5 = 12 ✓. Every one-step equation is this same move — undo what's been done to x, one step at a time.

questions.text: Check it! x + 7 = 15. What is x?

options.hint: That's adding 7 + 15. To undo “+7”, SUBTRACT 7 from both sides: 15 − 7 = ?

options.praise: ⭐ Correct — 15 − 7 = 8, and 8 + 7 = 15 ✓. Balance kept!

options.hint: Close — but check it: 7 + 7 = 14, not 15. x must make the left side equal 15 exactly.

options.t: Solving an equation means isolating the variable, and whatever operation is applied to one side must be applied to the other — the balance is never broken.
To solve an equation, move each number across the equals sign and flip its sign.
options.fix: Not quite — nothing moves by itself. The flipped sign is the visible result of applying the inverse operation to BOTH sides: x + 5 = 12 becomes x = 7 because 5 was subtracted from each side.

options.t: One side of an equation can be simplified on its own, provided you balance it at the end.
options.fix: Not quite — equality survives only if both sides change together at every step. Alter one side alone and it is a different equation, whose answer will fail the check: 7 + 5 = 12.

lessons.title: History: a thesis is a claim

steps.text: A history essay stands or falls on its thesis — and a thesis is a claim you must prove, not a topic. Weak: “This essay is about the transcontinental railroad.” That announces a subject; it argues nothing. Strong: “The transcontinental railroad reshaped American migration by cutting a six-month journey to one week.” Specific, arguable, and provable with evidence — every paragraph can now do a job.

questions.text: Check it! Which of these is a real thesis?

options.hint: That's a topic announcement — it claims nothing, so there's nothing to prove. A thesis takes a position evidence can support.

options.text: “Homesteading succeeded only where railroads arrived first, because access to markets decided which farms survived.”
options.praise: ⭐ Correct — a specific, arguable claim with a reason attached. That's a thesis an essay can prove.

options.hint: True, but it's a bare fact, not an argument — nobody could disagree, so there's nothing to prove. A thesis must be arguable.

options.t: A thesis is a specific, arguable claim that evidence can prove — it takes a position rather than announcing a topic or restating a settled fact.
A thesis is a clear statement of the topic the essay will discuss.
options.fix: Not quite — “This essay is about the transcontinental railroad” announces a subject and argues nothing. A thesis takes a position a reader could dispute — that the railroad reshaped migration — and every paragraph then works to prove it.

options.t: A thesis is strongest when it states a fact nobody can dispute.
options.fix: Not quite — an undisputed fact needs no essay; nobody writes five paragraphs proving the railroad was completed in 1869. A thesis must be arguable, because the argument is the essay.

steps.text: Memory research is blunt: retrieval practice beats re-reading. Forcing your brain to pull an answer out — flashcards, self-quizzing — strengthens the memory far more than looking at the page again, and spreading short sessions across days (spacing) beats one long cram. So ten minutes of self-testing a day beats one long Sunday cram.

questions.text: Check it! The night before a test, which method works best?

options.text: Re-read your notes for three hours
options.hint: It FEELS productive, but recognition isn't recall — on the test you must produce answers, not recognise them. Practise producing.

options.praise: ⭐ Correct — retrieval practice plus sleep. That's how memory research says to study.

options.hint: Highlighting marks what looks important without making you retrieve anything. Test yourself instead — that's the rep that counts.

options.t: Retrieval practice — pulling answers out of memory through self-testing, spaced across days — builds stronger memory than re-reading, because it trains the exact act a test demands.
Re-reading works best because repeated exposure makes the material feel familiar.
options.fix: Not quite — familiarity is recognition, and recognition is not recall. A test requires you to PRODUCE answers, not recognise them; self-testing is the repetition that trains production.

options.t: Highlighting is effective because it marks the important material for later review.
options.fix: Not quite — highlighting sorts the page without requiring any retrieval. The evidence favours the harder act: close the notes, pull the answer out, then check it — and let sleep consolidate it.

steps.text: DNA is the instruction set. Its code stays protected inside the nucleus, but proteins are built OUTSIDE it — a messenger copy (mRNA) carries one gene's instructions to a ribosome, which reads the code and assembles the matching protein, amino acid by amino acid. DNA → message → protein: that single flow runs everything from muscle fibre to insulin.

questions.text: Check it! Where in the cell are proteins actually assembled?

options.hint: Mitochondria make ATP — that's lesson 1. Protein assembly happens where the mRNA message gets read and built from.

options.praise: ⭐ Correct — ribosomes read the mRNA copy and build the protein. The central flow of biology, learned.

options.hint: The nucleus stores the DNA master copy, deliberately protected. Building happens outside it, at the organelle that reads the message.

options.t: DNA stays protected in the nucleus; an mRNA copy carries one gene's instructions to a ribosome, which reads the code and assembles the matching protein.
Proteins are assembled inside the nucleus, where the DNA instructions are stored.
options.fix: Not quite — the master copy never leaves the nucleus, and assembly never happens there. The mRNA messenger carries one gene's instructions out to a ribosome, where the protein is built.

options.t: The mitochondria read the DNA code and build proteins from it.
options.fix: Not quite — mitochondria produce ATP; they do not read genes. Protein synthesis belongs to the ribosome, working from the mRNA copy of the DNA code.

steps.text: Two-step equations just need the balance move twice — undo in reverse order, last thing on, first thing off. Worked example:
2x + 3 = 11 → subtract 3: 2x = 8 → divide by 2: x = 4
Check: 2 × 4 + 3 = 11 ✓. Undo the addition first, then the multiplication — every two-step equation follows exactly this order.

questions.text: Check it! 3x + 4 = 19. What is x?

options.hint: Check it: 3 × 6 + 4 = 22, not 19. Subtract 4 from both sides first: 3x = 15 — then divide by 3.

options.praise: ⭐ Correct — 3x = 15, so x = 5, and 3 × 5 + 4 = 19 ✓. Two steps, balance kept!

options.hint: Check it: 3 × 4 + 4 = 16, not 19. Undo the +4 first, then undo the ×3.

options.t: A two-step equation is solved by undoing the operations in reverse order — the addition or subtraction first, then the multiplication or division — applying each step to both sides.
In a two-step equation you divide first, because multiplication is the stronger operation.
options.fix: Not quite — the order is the reverse of how the expression was built: last operation on, first operation off. In 2x + 3 = 11 the +3 was applied last, so subtract 3 first (2x = 8), then divide by 2.

options.t: Once x is found, checking the answer is optional — the method guarantees it.
options.fix: Not quite — the check is part of the method: substitute back and the equation confirms itself (2 × 4 + 3 = 11 ✓). Skipping it leaves arithmetic slips invisible.

steps.text: Historians grade evidence by distance. A primary source was created AT the time, by someone who was there — a letter, a diary, a photograph, a ticket stub. A secondary source was made later, ABOUT the time — a textbook, a documentary, a museum label. An essay gets stronger the moment a primary source walks into it: real voices beat summaries of voices.

questions.text: Check it! Which of these is a PRIMARY source for a railroad-era essay?

options.text: A modern textbook chapter on westward expansion
options.hint: A textbook is written long afterwards, ABOUT the era — that's secondary. Primary means created at the time, by someone who was there.

options.text: A letter written by a railroad worker in 1869
options.praise: ⭐ Correct — written in 1869 by someone doing the work. That's evidence an essay can stand on.

options.text: A documentary film about the railroad
options.hint: A documentary is made later, however well researched — secondary. Look for the source created during the events themselves.

options.t: A primary source was created at the time of the events by someone who was there; a secondary source was created later, about those events — the distinction is distance, not quality.
A primary source is a reliable source, and a secondary source is one to avoid.
options.fix: Not quite — primary does not mean trustworthy, and secondary does not mean weak. A railroad worker's 1869 letter is primary because of when, and by whom, it was made; a rigorous modern textbook is secondary — and may still be excellent.

options.t: A letter or photograph becomes a secondary source once it is reprinted in a textbook.
options.fix: Not quite — reprinting changes the container, not the source. The 1869 letter remains primary wherever it appears; it is the textbook's own commentary around it that is secondary.

steps.text: In Spanish, regular -ar verbs change their ending to match WHO is acting. Take hablar (to speak): drop the -ar, then add — yo hablo, tú hablas, él/ella habla. Learn that one pattern and it unlocks hundreds of verbs: estudiar → estudio, bailar → bailo, trabajar → trabajo.

questions.text: Check it! Complete the sentence: «Yo ___ español.»

options.hint: HABLA is the él/ella ending. The subject of this sentence is YO — which ending matches “I”?

options.praise: ⭐ Correct — yo hablo. One pattern, hundreds of verbs unlocked.

options.hint: HABLAN belongs to ellos — “they”. The sentence's subject is YO (“I”), which takes the -o ending.

options.t: For regular -ar verbs, drop the -ar and add the ending that matches the subject: yo hablo, tú hablas, él habla — one pattern unlocks hundreds of verbs.
The verb ending stays the same for every subject; only the pronoun changes.
options.fix: Not quite — the ending is precisely what signals who is acting: hablo, hablas and habla are three forms of one verb. Spanish marks the subject on the verb itself.

options.t: Yo takes the -a ending, as in «yo habla».
options.fix: Not quite — -a belongs to él/ella: habla means he or she speaks. Yo takes -o: «yo hablo». The ending is matched to the subject, every time.
